newsitem.title: CHINA: China city cab drivers strike against new levy.
newsitem.headline: China city cab drivers strike against new levy.

text.p: Taxi drivers in the Chinese city Qingdao went on strike to protest against a new government levy, the latest in a series of rare cases of industrial action, drivers and officials said on Friday.

Cab operators in Qingdao city, in northern China's Shandong province, kerbed their cars on Tuesday and Wednesday to show their anger at a 10,000 ($1,200) yuan levy recently announced by the city government, they said.
"We went on strike for two days," said one driver. "Everyone is angry at the fee... it's too much."
The unofficial action was led by staff at some of Qingdao's largest taxi companies and was backed by almost all the city's cab operators, said the driver, who did not want to be identified.
The stoppage followed similar action by dissatisfied drivers in cities across northern China, including the port city of Tianjin and the Shandong provincial capital of Jinan, he said.
Industrial action is rare in China, where all labour unions are controlled by the ruling Communist Party and breaches of worker discipline are quickly quelled.
Controls on industrial action did not apply to taxis, which although officially registered with cab companies, could just simply leave the road to make their point, the driver said.
"It isn't like a factory going on strike... we just stay at home. There's nothing they can do," he said.
City officials dismissed the action as poorly organised, weakly suported and unlikely to change municipal policy.
"I don't think there is any chance of this rule being changed," said one official. "This is not a real action, it's just some people stopping driving.
"It's not a strike. A strike is illegal," said the official who declined to be identified.

A surplus of taxis in Qingdao, a former German-run concession blessed with golden beaches and a temperate climate, forced the city to auction new licences for would-be drivers for around 100,000 yuan, he said.

With new drivers paying such a hefty fee, the levy on existing drivers was very reasonable, he said. The levy is believed to be a one-off payment although it possibly could be once every several years.

Some drivers continued to operate during the stoppage, sometimes sticking to suburban roads out of fear of attack from striking colleagues in the city centre, but residents said the strike appeared remarkably solid.
"You couldn't see a taxi anywhere," said a shop attendant at the city airport. "It seemed 100 percent."

The action appeared inspired at least partly by the success of their colleagues in Jinan city, where thousands of taxi drivers earlier this month ended a three-day work stoppage after the municipal government met protesters and agreed to lower fees.
While some Qingdao drivers joked about holding public demonstrations to back their protest against the new levy, one driver said such talk could never turn to action.
"Nobody dares demonstrate. People get detained when they demonstrate," he said.
